mainTopic: What does ״מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ״ forbid: one side, both sides, or no food at all? (Reworking the views of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא and שמואל)
overview: This amud asks what happens when someone says ״מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ״ ("I am avowed from you"). First the גמרא says that this plain phrase forbids both people, and it backs this up with רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא. A משנה about ״הריני עליך חרם״ seems to forbid only one side, and the גמרא answers twice that the speaker there spelled out that the other side stays permitted. But the end of that משנה implies that a plain vow forbids only one side. So the גמרא re-states רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא: ״מודר אני לך״ forbids both people, while ״מודרני הימך״ forbids only the speaker. This clashes with how שמואל's words on our משנה were explained, so the גמרא re-states שמואל as being about eating versus all benefit. That reading does not fit שמואל's wording ״עד שיאמר״. In the final version, the plain phrases do not forbid food at all, because each one naturally means a different kind of separation: no talking, no business, or not standing within four אמות. Only adding "that I eat" or "that I taste" makes it a food vow.

steps.title: Saying only "I am avowed from you" forbids both people
steps.stepSummary: If a person says only ״מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ״ and adds nothing, both people are forbidden to benefit from each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said just "I am avowed from you" by itself, both of them are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is laying out the plain case in שמואל's approach: the short phrase ״מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ״ with nothing added makes both people forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ״אֲבָל״ ("but") sets this plain case against versions where the speaker spelled out who may not eat from whom. When nothing is spelled out, the separation goes both ways. The idea seems to be that "I am separated from you" cuts the connection from both sides.

keyTerms.meaning: "I am avowed (separated by a vow) from you"
by itself, alone, with nothing added
both of them are forbidden

phrases.english: But if he said "I am avowed from you" by itself,
phrases.notes: "By itself" means he did not add who is forbidden to eat from whom.

phrases.english: both of them are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of שמואל's view and gives the rule for the plain, unspecified phrase.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A plain ״מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ״ forbids both people from benefiting from each other.

steps.title: Support from רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא
steps.stepSummary: The rule matches a statement of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, who said that ״מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ״ forbids both people.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is like what רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: "I am avowed from you" means both are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that the rule it just gave is not new. An אמורא, רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, already said the same thing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase ״כִּי הָא״ ("like this") links the rule to a known statement. Now the rule rests on a named authority, not only on reasoning. This also sets it up as a target for the challenge that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: "like that which [so-and-so] said": links a rule to a known statement
an אמורא from ארץ ישראל, son of רבי חנינא

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: This is like what רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said:
"I am avowed from you": both of them are forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up the rule of Step 1 with a named statement.
steps.raayaObject: The rule that a plain ״מוּדְּרַנִי הֵימָךְ״ forbids both sides.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The statement of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא.

steps.title: Challenge from a משנה: "I am חרם to you" forbids only one side
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says that with ״הֲרֵינִי עָלֶיךָ חֵרֶם״ only the other person is forbidden, not the speaker. Why aren't both forbidden?
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה: "I am חרם to you": the one the vow is about is forbidden, but the one who made the vow is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a משנה that seems to clash with the rule that both people are forbidden. It says only one side becomes forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ״הֲרֵינִי עָלֶיךָ חֵרֶם״ the speaker makes himself forbidden to the other person, so the other person may not benefit from him. The משנה says the speaker himself is still allowed to benefit from the other. If a vow like this forbids both sides, as in Steps 1-2, the speaker should be forbidden too.

keyTerms.meaning: "we learned" in a משנה: brings a משנה as a source
something dedicated to the בית המקדש, and so forbidden for personal use
the person the vow is said about, who becomes forbidden
the person who makes the vow against the other

steps.confusionAlert: Keep the two people apart. The מַדִּיר / נוֹדֵר is the speaker who makes the vow. The מוּדָּר is the other person the vow is said about. In this case only the מוּדָּר is forbidden.

phrases.english: We learned in a משנה: "I am hereby חרם to you":
phrases.notes: This משנה comes later in the מסכת (47b). He means "benefiting from me is like benefiting from Temple property."

phrases.english: the one the vow is about is forbidden,
but the one who made the vow is not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule of Steps 1-2 using a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that this kind of vow forbids both people.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says only the מוּדָּר is forbidden, but under שמואל's view the speaker should be forbidden too.

steps.title: The משנה is a case where he said the other side stays permitted
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about a speaker who said out loud, "but you are not forbidden to me."
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where he spelled it out: "and you are not [חרם] to me."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the משנה to a special case where the speaker clearly left himself permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the speaker openly says the other person is not forbidden to him, then of course only one side is forbidden. So the משנה does not cover a plain, unspecified vow. The rule of Steps 1-2 for the plain case still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: "for example, where he spelled it out": limits a source to a special case
"and you are not [forbidden] to me"

phrases.english: It is a case where he spelled it out: "and you are not to me."
phrases.notes: Meaning: "you are not חרם to me," so the speaker may still benefit from the other person.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a special case (the speaker spelled out his wording).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to be about a plain vow, where only one side would be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a vow where the speaker clearly said the other side stays permitted.

steps.title: Second challenge: "You are חרם to me" forbids only the speaker
steps.stepSummary: The same משנה says that with ״אַתְּ עָלַי חֵרֶם״ only the speaker is forbidden. Why isn't the other person forbidden too?
steps.simpleTranslation: "You are חרם to me": the one who made the vow is forbidden, but the one the vow is about is not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings the next part of the same משנה, the opposite case, and asks the same kind of question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the speaker makes the other person forbidden to himself, so the speaker may not benefit from the other. The משנה says the other person is still allowed to benefit from the speaker. Under the both-sides rule, he should be forbidden too.

keyTerms.meaning: the one who makes the vow (the speaker)
"you are to me": the speaker forbids the other person to himself

phrases.english: "You are חרם to me":
the one who made the vow is forbidden, but the one the vow is about is not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel challenge from the next case in the same משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that this kind of vow forbids both people.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה says only the speaker is forbidden, but under שמואל's view the other person should be forbidden too.

steps.title: Again, a case where he said the other side stays permitted
steps.stepSummary: This too is a case where the speaker said out loud, "but I am not forbidden to you."
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where he spelled it out: "and I am not [חרם] to you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same kind of answer as before: the משנה is about a speaker who clearly left the other person permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the speaker openly said he is not forbidden to the other person, only one side is forbidden. So this part of the משנה also says nothing about the plain case.

keyTerms.meaning: "and I am not [forbidden] to you"

phrases.english: It is a case where he spelled it out: "and I am not to you."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 5, in the same way as Step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a special case (the speaker spelled out his wording).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: This case seemed to be about a plain vow forbidding only the speaker.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is about a vow where the speaker clearly said the other person stays permitted.

steps.title: The end of the משנה suggests a plain vow forbids only one side
steps.stepSummary: The end of the משנה says both are forbidden only when the speaker says "I am to you and you are to me." That suggests a plain vow forbids only one side, which goes against שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: But in a plain case, what happens? Both are forbidden? Yet the end of the משנה teaches: "I am to you and you are to me": both are forbidden. So it is in this case that both are forbidden, but in a plain case, he is forbidden and the other is permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the earlier answers with a stronger question taken from the end of the same משנה. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a plain vow already forbade both sides, the משנה would not need a special case of "I am to you and you are to me" to make both forbidden. Since the משנה needs that double wording to forbid both, a plain vow must forbid only one side. This attacks שמואל's rule directly, not just through the earlier, narrower cases.

keyTerms.meaning: a plain case, with nothing spelled out
"since the end of the משנה teaches": a proof from the last part of a source
"it is this [case]": only in this case
permitted

steps.whatToRemember: The answers "he spelled it out" protected שמואל from the first two cases of the משנה. But the last case (״הריני עליך ואת עלי״) implies that a plain vow forbids only one side. This is a direct challenge to the rule that both people are forbidden.
steps.confusionAlert: The question ״אֲבָל סְתָמָא מַאי? שְׁנֵיהֶן אֲסוּרִים״ is not a real question looking for information. It states שמואל's view in order to show that the משנה goes against it.

phrases.english: But in a plain case, what? Both are forbidden?
But since the end of the משנה teaches:
"I am hereby to you and you are to me": both are forbidden,
it is in this case that both are forbidden,

phrases.aramaic: הָא סְתָמָא — הוּא אָסוּר וַחֲבֵרוֹ מוּתָּר!
phrases.english: but in a plain case, he is forbidden and the other is permitted!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל סְתָמָא מַאי שְׁנֵיהֶן אֲסוּרִים הָא מִדְּקָתָנֵי סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows that the answers of Steps 4 and 6 are not enough, using an inference from the end of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's rule (Steps 1-2) that a plain vow forbids both people.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The end of the משנה needs special double wording to forbid both people. So a plain vow must forbid only one side.

steps.title: Re-stating the view of רבי יוסי son of רבי חנינא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-states רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's view: "מודר אני לך" forbids both people, but "מודרני הימך" forbids only the speaker.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is how רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's view was stated: If someone says "I am avowed to you," both of them are forbidden. If he says "I am avowed from you," he is forbidden and the other person is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 7 by saying we had the earlier view wrong. It re-states the view so that it depends on the exact wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new version splits the wording in two. "לך" (to you) makes the vow work both ways, so both are forbidden. "הימך" (from you) only moves away from the other person, so only the speaker is forbidden. This lets the משנה cases that forbid only one side fit, since they can be read as using one-sided wording.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is how it was stated (the earlier version is replaced)
I am avowed to you
I am avowed from you
Both of them are forbidden
And his fellow is permitted

steps.confusionAlert: The two phrases look almost the same, but the small word matters. "לך" (to you) forbids both people. "הימך" (from you) forbids only the speaker.

phrases.english: Rather, this is how it was stated
the view of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina:
"I am avowed to you"
both of them are forbidden;
"I am avowed from you"
phrases.notes: הֵימָךְ is just another way of saying "from you," the same as מִמְּךָ.

phrases.english: he is forbidden and his fellow is permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא הָכִי אִתְּמַר דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 7 by re-stating the earlier view so it depends on the exact wording.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-statement of an earlier view (the reported version is replaced)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A plain vow was thought to forbid both sides no matter how it was worded.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only "לך" (to you) forbids both. "הימך" (from you) forbids only the speaker.

steps.title: The משנה's "from you" was explained as forbidding both
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that we already explained the משנה, according to שמואל, as saying "מודרני הימך" forbids both people. That contradicts the new version.
steps.simpleTranslation: But our משנה teaches "from you," and we explained it according to שמואל: in all these cases, only when he says "that I taste of yours" or "that I eat of yours" is he forbidden while the other is permitted. But with "I am avowed from you," both are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new version from Step 8. It points out that "הימך" was earlier explained, according to שמואל, as forbidding both people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 said "הימך" forbids only the speaker. But the way we read our משנה according to שמואל, plain "מודרני הימך" forbids both. Only the added words "I eat" or "I taste" limit it to one side. So the new version clashes with שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: But our משנה (introduces a challenge)
And we explained it (as dealing with a certain case or view)
That which I taste of yours
That which I eat of yours

phrases.english: But our mishna teaches "from you,"
and we explained the mishna according to Shmuel:
phrases.notes: This points back to how the גמרא explained שמואל's words on the משנה on the previous amud (4b).

phrases.english: in all of them, only when he says
"that which I taste of yours"
or "that which I eat of yours,"
is he forbidden and his fellow permitted;
but with "I am avowed from you,"
both are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the new version in Step 8 using the earlier explanation of the משנה according to שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 8 that "מודרני הימך" forbids only the speaker.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: According to שמואל, plain "מודרני הימך" forbids both. Only adding "I eat" or "I taste" limits it to one side. So "הימך" cannot forbid only the speaker.

steps.title: שמואל's rule was about eating versus all benefit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-states שמואל's words: "I eat" or "I taste" forbids only eating, while plain "מודרני ממך" forbids all benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, שמואל's statement was originally said like this: The reason he is forbidden only to eat is that he said "that I eat of yours" or "that I taste of yours." But if he said "I am avowed from you," he is forbidden even to get any benefit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 9 by re-stating שמואל's own words. It says his rule was never about who is forbidden. It was about how much is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, שמואל's words seemed to separate a one-sided vow from a vow that forbids both people. Now they separate eating from all benefit. "I eat" or "I taste" limits the vow to food. Plain "מודרני ממך" covers every kind of benefit. So שמואל no longer says anything about "הימך" forbidding both, and the clash with Step 8 goes away.

keyTerms.meaning: From the start, originally
The reason
Eating
Benefit (any kind of use or enjoyment)

steps.whatToRemember: In this new version, שמואל's words about "I eat" or "I taste" decide how much is forbidden (only eating, or all benefit), not who is forbidden.

phrases.english: Rather, from the start
Shmuel's statement was stated like this:
The reason is that he said "that which I eat of yours"
or "that which I taste of yours"

phrases.aramaic: הוּא דְּאֵין הוּא אָסוּר אֶלָּא בַּאֲכִילָה.
phrases.english: that he is forbidden only in eating.
But "I am avowed from you"
he is forbidden even in benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 9 by re-stating שמואל so his words no longer deal with who is forbidden.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל's words were about whether one person or both are forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: שמואל's words are about eating only versus all benefit.

steps.title: If so, why didn't שמואל phrase it more simply?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if שמואל meant only eating versus benefit, he should have said it directly, "if he said only 'I eat' or 'I taste,' only eating is forbidden."
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, שמואל should have said it this way: And if he said only "that I eat of yours" or "that I taste of yours," only eating is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the new version from Step 10 based on how שמואל worded his statement. Step 12 answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's words were "בכולן עד שיאמר" (in all of them, only when he says). That sounds like the added words are needed for the vow to work in a certain way. If he only meant that these words limit the vow to eating, a plain "if he said only..." would have been the natural way to say it. So the wording does not seem to fit the new reading.

keyTerms.meaning: If so (introduces a challenge from what was just said)
Let him say (he should have said)

phrases.english: If so,
let Shmuel say it this way:
and if he said only
"that which I eat of yours"
or "that which I taste of yours,"
he is forbidden only in eating.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the new version of שמואל in Step 10 based on how he worded his statement.
steps.kashyaTarget: The new version of שמואל's statement in Step 10.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: שמואל's actual wording, "in all of them, only when he says," does not match the meaning the new version gives it. If he meant that these words limit the vow to eating, he should have said "if he said only..."

steps.title: שמואל's statement is given in a new final version
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא re-states שמואל: food is forbidden only because the speaker added "I eat" or "I taste." A plain "מודרני הימך" does not suggest a food ban at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is how שמואל's words were said: the reason the person is forbidden is that he said "that which I eat of yours" or "that which I taste of yours." But if he only said "I am avowed from you," that does not show he meant to forbid himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the version of שמואל that was just challenged and gives a new one. Food is forbidden only because the speaker added the words about eating or tasting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 asked why שמואל said "only when he says" (עד שיאמר) and not "if he said only...", which would mean the added words merely limit the vow to eating. The answer is that the added words do not limit anything. They are what create the food ban in the first place. Without them, a plain "מודרני הימך" does not point to food at all. That is why שמואל needed the wording "only when he says."

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is how it was said. This introduces a corrected version of a statement.
That which I eat of yours. This wording connects the vow to food.
That which I taste of yours
It does not imply or suggest

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix this up with Step 10. There, a plain "מודרני" was thought to forbid all benefit. Now the plain phrase is said not to point to food at all.

phrases.english: Rather, this is how it was stated:
The reason is that he said "that which I eat of yours"
or "that which I taste of yours,"
that is why he is forbidden.
But if he said only "I am avowed from you,"
it does not suggest that he said he is forbidden.
phrases.notes: He means forbidden to eat his friend's food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 11 by giving a corrected version of שמואל's statement.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-stating what the אמורא actually said
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל contrasted food ("I eat") with all benefit (plain "מודרני").
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the added words "I eat" or "I taste" forbid food. Plain "מודרני הימך" does not suggest a food ban.

steps.title: Why the plain phrases do not mean food
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that each plain phrase from the משנה naturally means a different kind of separation: no talking, no business, or not standing within four אמות.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? "I am avowed from you" suggests "I won't talk with you." "I am separated from you" suggests "I won't do business with you." "I am distanced from you" suggests "I won't stand within four אמות of you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why a plain phrase does not forbid food, and then answers. Each of the three phrases from the משנה has its own natural meaning, and none of them is about eating.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each phrase could be describing a different kind of keeping apart. So without the words "I eat" or "I taste," we cannot assume the person meant food. This is why the added words are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the reason?
I will not speak with you
I am separated from you
Business dealings, literally taking and giving
I am distanced from you
Four אמות, a person's personal space

steps.whatToRemember: In the final version of שמואל, the plain phrases מודרני, מופרשני and מרוחקני do not by themselves forbid food. Each could mean another kind of separation. Only adding "that I eat" or "that I taste" makes it a food vow.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
"I am avowed from you"
suggests "I will not speak with you."
"I am separated from you"
phrases.notes: This phrase and the next one are the other two phrases listed in the משנה.

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא עָבֵידְנָא עִמָּךְ מַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן מַשְׁמַע.
phrases.english: suggests that I will not do business with you.
"I am distanced from you"

phrases.aramaic: דְּלָא קָאֵימְנָא בְּאַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת דִּילָךְ מַשְׁמַע.
phrases.english: suggests that I will not stand within your four cubits.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason behind the new version of שמואל in Step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why a plain "מודרני הימך" does not suggest a food ban.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Each plain phrase naturally means a different separation: not talking, not doing business, or not standing within four אמות.
